title: Clinical impact and misdiagnosis of functional ophthalmological symptoms: a case report
case_prompt:
A 42-year-old Caucasian woman was referred for a review of her disability benefits. From age 31, she had persistent left facial pain diagnosed as trigeminal neuralgia. Treatments included glycerol injection of Gasser’s ganglion, microvascular decompression, stereotactic radiosurgery targeting the trigeminal root, brainstem, and hippocampus, and subcutaneous infra- and supraorbital electrode implantation; none provided lasting relief. She stopped working at age 32 and initially received full disability benefits.

At age 36, she noted visual disturbances that progressed over 12 months to complete blindness by age 39. On examination at age 42, she reported no light perception bilaterally. Ocular findings were limited to severe punctate superficial keratitis with anesthesia of the left cornea; the right cornea was normal. Funduscopic examination showed normal macula, retina, vessels, and optic nerves in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography of the macula and optic nerve was normal. Electrophysiological studies, including multifocal and full-field electroretinography and pattern visual evoked potentials, were within normal limits. Brain imaging and blood tests revealed no abnormalities to explain her loss of vision.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Essential trigeminal neuralgia — “after ten years of treatment-resistant evolution (including highly invasive treatments) and unremarkable investigations, we ruled out essential trigeminal neuralgia.”  
2. Neuropathic pain or cluster headache — “We also ruled out neuropathic pain or a cluster headache.”  
3. Organic ocular or visual pathway disease — “detailed ophthalmological and neurological examination, electrophysiology testing, brain imaging, and blood tests revealed no significant abnormalities that could have contributed to his visual impairment.”  
4. Vitamin B12 deficiency — “We concluded that the moderate vitamin B12 deficiency presented by our patient had no relationship with her reduced visual acuity.”  
5. Alcohol-related visual impairment — “the patient was asked about alcohol consumption during the interview, and the answer was negative … there is no trace of a history of alcohol consumption and liver function test showed normal values.”  
6. Factitious disorder or simulation — “There was no argument for a factitious disorder or a simulation, depressive reaction, or other psychiatric diagnoses.”  
7. Dissociative neurological symptom disorder with visual disturbance — “The thorough psychiatric examination … concluded … the diagnosis of a dissociative neurological symptom disorder with visual disturbance.”
final_diagnosis: Dissociative neurological symptom disorder with visual disturbance
